understand.plain: Without a named owner, OSS governance defaults to whoever made the last decision or, more often, to no one at all. In a cloud-delivered stack that gap is wider than it looks: open source arrives through application code, base images, deployment pipelines and managed services, and where ownership exists it often stops at the application layer.

regulatoryHook.plain: The CRA requires manufacturers of products with digital elements to operate defined vulnerability handling and compliance processes. Those processes presuppose clear internal responsibility; undefined ownership is a structural gap against that expectation.
regulatoryHook.boundary: Signpost only. This does not decide whether the CRA applies to you. Confirm with a qualified specialist.

act.1: Name one person, even informally, as the point of contact for OSS questions. Write their name somewhere shared and accessible to the team.
act.2: Document the OSS owner in a team wiki or repository README. Define what decisions they are consulted on.
act.3: Formalise the role with a written remit that covers the application, base image and pipeline layers, plus the managed services you consume. Include it in relevant role descriptions.
act.4: Ensure the owner role is part of succession planning and onboarding documentation so it survives staff turnover.

understand.plain: If you do not know what open source software is in your stack, it is harder to respond to vulnerabilities, answer customer security questions or produce an accurate SBOM. A normal dependency file may only show application libraries. It may not include software inside container images, sidecars added at deployment, deployment tools or managed services.

regulatoryHook.plain: If you place a product with digital elements on the EU market, you will need an SBOM. SBOM obligations under the CRA apply from December 2027.
regulatoryHook.boundary: Signpost only. This does not decide whether the CRA applies to you. Confirm with a qualified specialist.

act.1: Generate a first inventory from your existing build tooling and save it somewhere shared. Include the base image, not just the application manifest.
act.2: Pick an SBOM format (SPDX or CycloneDX) and produce one SBOM for your main product that covers the container image as well as the application layer.
act.3: Generate the SBOM inside the build pipeline on every build rather than auditing a running environment that the next deployment will replace, and assign an owner to keep it current.

understand.plain: Consistent, documented OSS adoption decisions protect the organisation from licence conflicts, security risks, and costly reversals when ad hoc choices accumulate over time. Cloud environments add a second route in: components enter through pipeline configuration and infrastructure-as-code modules, not just application dependencies, and those routes usually get less review.

act.1: Write a one-page checklist: what questions must be answered before adopting a new OSS component? Licence, maintenance status, and security record are the minimum. Make it explicit that pipeline actions and infrastructure modules count as components.
act.2: Circulate the checklist and apply it to one real adoption decision as a pilot, with the owner signing off.
act.3: Embed the checklist in procurement templates and new developer onboarding materials so it becomes routine.

understand.plain: Unmonitored OSS dependencies are a primary attack surface. Incidents such as Log4Shell showed that organisations without dependency visibility cannot respond quickly when a critical vulnerability is disclosed. On rented infrastructure there is a second question: which components do you patch, and which does your provider patch? Where that is never written down, components get missed, and an organisation can rate itself higher than the evidence supports by assuming the provider covers something it does not.

regulatoryHook.instrument: Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) and NIS2 Directive
regulatoryHook.plain: The CRA requires manufacturers to actively monitor for vulnerabilities and provide timely security updates, with reporting obligations for actively exploited vulnerabilities applying from 11 September 2026. NIS2 requires essential and important entities to manage security in their supply chains, including OSS dependencies, and cloud service providers covered by NIS2 may pass their own supply chain requirements down to customers through contracts.
regulatoryHook.boundary: Signpost only. This does not decide whether the CRA or NIS2 applies to you. Confirm with a qualified specialist.

act.1: Enable Dependabot or equivalent automated vulnerability alerts on your main repositories today, and switch on image scanning for your base images.
act.2: Assign a named triage owner, set a target response time (for example 72 hours for critical advisories), and write down the managed and self-managed split: for each important component, who patches it, you or the provider?
act.3: Define a vulnerability handling procedure that covers transitive dependencies and scheduled base image rebuilds, and test it with a real advisory.

learn.title: Grype (vulnerability scanner for images and SBOMs)

understand.plain: OSS licences carry obligations. Using a GPL-licensed component in a commercial product without understanding the implications can trigger copyleft obligations or breach a customer contract. Base images carry licences too: if you distribute a container built from a base image you did not create, you may be taking on licensing obligations that have never been reviewed.

act.1: Run a licence scan across your main repositories and your base images using a free tool such as REUSE, scancode-toolkit, or Syft's licence output.
act.2: Assign a licence owner and create a short list of accepted, for-review, and rejected licences for your context.
act.3: Embed licence checking in your CI pipeline so new components are licence-checked before adoption as routine.

understand.plain: EU instruments including the Cyber Resilience Act and the NIS2 Directive place obligations on organisations in relation to open source components. The first step is identifying which instruments may apply to your role in the ecosystem. For an SME offering a hosted product, the first question is whether the product falls within the scope of the CRA at all, which depends more on how the hosted service forms part of the product than on where the software runs.

regulatoryHook.plain: Manufacturers and distributors of products with digital elements face obligations under the CRA. Products with digital elements can include remote data processing where that service is an essential part of the product, so a hosted application may be in scope even if nothing is installed on the customer's device. Under Article 71 of Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, obligations to report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents apply from 11 September 2026; the main obligations, including SBOM requirements, apply from 11 December 2027.
regulatoryHook.boundary: Signpost only. This does not decide whether the CRA applies to you. Confirm with a qualified specialist.

act.1: Identify which EU instruments may apply to your organisation (CRA, NIS2, AI Act) and log your initial assessment with the date.
act.2: Map your regulatory role: are you a user, distributor, or steward of OSS components or products? If you deliver a hosted product, record your initial view on whether it falls within CRA scope and treat that as an early governance question rather than a late legal one.
act.3: Track the regulatory timeline (CRA vulnerability reporting from 11 September 2026; main obligations including SBOM from 11 December 2027), note any supply chain requirements your cloud providers pass down through contracts, and assign ownership of compliance readiness to a named role.

understand.plain: Contributing code without clear rules can create licence, intellectual property and reputational risks. There is also a maintenance risk when your team changes open source software locally but never contributes those changes back. Over time, your version can become harder to update and maintain.

act.1: Identify the five OSS projects most critical to your product, including any base images and infrastructure modules you have forked or patched locally, and assess their community health using CHAOSS metrics or equivalent.
act.2: Draft a one-page contribution policy covering who may contribute, to what projects, and under what conditions.
act.3: Formalise your contribution approach with clear contributor agreement guidance, including a Contributor Licence Agreement (CLA) where one is needed, and assign an upstream engagement owner.
